tests.title: 01 · Ownership and moves
tests.description: Who owns a value, when it moves, and when it is dropped.

options: It doesn't compile: `s1` was moved into `s2`
It compiles but panics at run time
questions.answer: It doesn't compile: `s1` was moved into `s2`
questions.explanation: `String` isn't `Copy`, so `let s2 = s1;` moves ownership. Using `s1` afterwards is error E0382 (borrow of moved value).

questions.question: Which of these types are `Copy`? Choose all that apply.
questions.explanation: Scalars, and tuples and arrays of `Copy` types, are `Copy`, as are shared references. Types that own heap memory (String, Vec, Box) are not.

questions.question: Which trait must a type implement so that assignment copies it instead of moving it?
questions.explanation: `Copy` types are duplicated bit for bit on assignment. `Copy` requires `Clone`, and only types whose bitwise copy is a valid, independent value may implement it.

questions.question: Can a type implement both `Copy` and `Drop`?
options: Yes, and `drop` runs once per copy
questions.answer: No, the compiler rejects it
questions.explanation: Error E0184: implicit copies would make it ambiguous how many times the destructor should run, so `Copy` and `Drop` are mutually exclusive.

questions.question: Locals `a`, `b` and `c` are declared in that order. In what order are they dropped at the end of the scope?
questions.answer: c, b, a
questions.explanation: Local variables are dropped in reverse order of declaration, so later values can safely refer to earlier ones.

questions.question: In what order are a struct's fields dropped?
options: In declaration order, after the struct's own `Drop::drop` runs
questions.answer: In declaration order, after the struct's own `Drop::drop` runs
questions.explanation: Fields, tuple elements and array elements drop in order; unlike locals, they are not reversed.

questions.question: A function takes `v: Vec<i32>` by value. After `f(v)`, what can the caller do with `v`?
options: Nothing: it was moved into the function
Read it but not change it
Use it as before; the Vec was copied
questions.answer: Nothing: it was moved into the function
questions.explanation: Passing by value moves ownership. The callee drops the vector at its end unless it hands it back.

questions.question: Name the method that explicitly makes a deep copy of a `String`.
questions.explanation: `clone` is an explicit, possibly expensive copy; `Copy` is implicit and reserved for cheap bitwise copies.

questions.question: What does `std::mem::take(&mut v)` do when `v` is a `Vec<T>`?
options: Returns the vector and leaves an empty `Vec` in its place
Moves `v` out and leaves it uninitialized
questions.answer: Returns the vector and leaves an empty `Vec` in its place
questions.explanation: `mem::take` swaps in `Default::default()` and returns the old value: the usual way to move out of a `&mut` field.

questions.question: Which function moves a value out from behind a `&mut T` by putting a given replacement in its place?
questions.answer: `std::mem::replace`
questions.explanation: `mem::replace(dest, new)` returns the old value. `ptr::read` is `unsafe` and would duplicate ownership.

questions.question: Is leaking memory, for example with `std::mem::forget` or an `Rc` cycle, allowed in safe Rust?
options: Yes: leaks are memory-safe, so safe code may leak
questions.answer: Yes: leaks are memory-safe, so safe code may leak
questions.explanation: Rust guarantees no use-after-free and no data races, not that destructors run. `mem::forget` is safe, so unsafe code must never rely on `Drop` running for soundness.
Destructuring moved `t.0` (a String) but only copied `t.1` (an i32). A partially moved value's remaining fields stay usable.

questions.question: What happens to a value when its owner goes out of scope?
options: Its `Drop` implementation, if any, runs and its resources are freed right away
A garbage collector frees it later
It leaks unless dropped by hand
It moves to a global pool
questions.answer: Its `Drop` implementation, if any, runs and its resources are freed right away
questions.explanation: Deterministic destruction (RAII): resources are released at a known point, which is why guards, files and locks close promptly.

questions.question: Why can't you call `x.drop()` directly on a value whose type implements `Drop`?
options: It would run the destructor twice; call `std::mem::drop(x)` instead
questions.answer: It would run the destructor twice; call `std::mem::drop(x)` instead
questions.explanation: Error E0040. `mem::drop` just takes ownership, so the value goes out of scope at the end of that function.

questions.question: `let a = Box::new(5); let b = a;` How many heap allocations exist afterwards, and who owns it?
options: None; the box is optimized away by the language rules
questions.answer: One allocation, owned by `b`
questions.explanation: Moving a Box copies the pointer, not the heap value. Ownership transfers; `a` can no longer be used.

tests.title: 02 · Borrowing and references
tests.description: Shared and mutable references, and the rules the borrow checker enforces.

questions.question: Which borrowing rule does Rust enforce at any point in time?
options: Either one mutable reference or any number of shared references
Any number of mutable and shared references
One shared and one mutable reference at most
Only one reference of any kind
questions.answer: Either one mutable reference or any number of shared references
questions.explanation: Aliasing XOR mutability: this is what rules out data races and iterator invalidation at compile time.

options: It doesn't compile: `v` is borrowed while `push` needs `&mut v`
questions.answer: It doesn't compile: `v` is borrowed while `push` needs `&mut v`
questions.explanation: `push` may reallocate and leave `first` dangling, so the borrow checker rejects it (E0502).

questions.question: With non-lexical lifetimes (NLL), how long does a borrow last?
options: Until the end of the enclosing block
Until the end of the function
Until the borrowed value is dropped
questions.answer: Until its last use
questions.explanation: Since the 2018 edition, borrows end at their last use, which lets much more natural code compile.

questions.question: How is `&mut T` best described?
options: A reference that can be copied freely
A reference to a mutable global
A raw pointer with a lifetime
questions.answer: An exclusive (unique) reference
questions.explanation: `&mut` guarantees no other live access for its lifetime; mutation is a consequence of that uniqueness.

questions.question: Is `&T` `Copy`?
questions.answer: Yes, for every `T`
questions.explanation: Shared references are `Copy`. `&mut T` is not: it is moved, or implicitly reborrowed.

questions.question: What is a reborrow?
options: A new, shorter-lived reference made from an existing `&mut`, such as `&mut *r`, often implicit when passing `r` to a function
Borrowing the same value mutably twice
questions.answer: A new, shorter-lived reference made from an existing `&mut`, such as `&mut *r`, often implicit when passing `r` to a function
questions.explanation: Implicit reborrowing is why you can pass `r: &mut T` to a function and still use `r` afterwards.

options: It doesn't compile: it returns a reference to a local variable
It leaks `s` so the reference stays valid
questions.answer: It doesn't compile: it returns a reference to a local variable
questions.explanation: `s` is dropped when the function returns, so the reference would dangle. Return the `String` itself instead.

questions.question: Can you hold `&mut s.x` and `&mut s.y`, two different fields, at the same time?
options: Yes: borrows of disjoint fields are tracked separately
No, the whole struct is borrowed
questions.answer: Yes: borrows of disjoint fields are tracked separately
questions.explanation: The checker tracks borrow paths. It can't see through methods, though: `s.x_mut()` and `s.y_mut()` each borrow all of `s`.

questions.question: Which slice method splits a mutable slice into two non-overlapping mutable slices at an index?
questions.explanation: `split_at_mut(mid)` returns `(&mut [T], &mut [T])`; internally it uses `unsafe`, soundly, because the halves can't overlap.

questions.question: Why does `s.len()` work when `s: &&String`?
options: Method calls dereference the receiver automatically as many times as needed
questions.answer: Method calls dereference the receiver automatically as many times as needed
questions.explanation: Auto-deref applies to the receiver of a method call; `Deref` coercion also turns `&String` into `&str` in arguments.

questions.question: What is the type of `&v[1..3]` when `v: Vec<i32>`?
questions.explanation: Range indexing a Vec gives a slice, `[i32]`; borrowing it gives a fat pointer, `&[i32]`.

options: Two mutable borrows of `s` are alive at once, since `r1` is used after `r2` is made
questions.answer: Two mutable borrows of `s` are alive at once, since `r1` is used after `r2` is made
questions.explanation: `r1` is still live when `r2` is created. If `r1` weren't used afterwards, NLL would accept it.

questions.question: Why does `v.push(v.len())` compile even though `push` takes `&mut v`?
options: Two-phase borrows: the `&mut v` is reserved first, so `v.len()` can take a shared borrow before it's used
`len` returns a copy of the whole Vec
questions.answer: Two-phase borrows: the `&mut v` is reserved first, so `v.len()` can take a shared borrow before it's used
questions.explanation: Two-phase borrowing makes this common pattern of method arguments that read the receiver compile.

questions.question: Which of these can make a value mutable through a shared reference `&T`?
options: Interior mutability types such as `Cell`, `RefCell`, `Mutex` or atomics
questions.answer: Interior mutability types such as `Cell`, `RefCell`, `Mutex` or atomics
questions.explanation: Interior mutability is built on `UnsafeCell`; converting `&T` to `&mut T` yourself is always undefined behaviour.

tests.title: 03 · Lifetimes
tests.description: Lifetime annotations, elision, bounds and variance.

questions.question: What does a lifetime annotation like `'a` do?
options: It describes how long references must stay valid relative to each other; it doesn't change how long any value lives
It extends how long a value lives
It delays when a value is dropped
questions.answer: It describes how long references must stay valid relative to each other; it doesn't change how long any value lives
questions.explanation: Lifetimes are constraints the borrow checker verifies. They never change run-time behaviour.

questions.question: Which signature needs explicit lifetime annotations?
questions.answer: `fn longest(x: &str, y: &str) -> &str`
questions.explanation: With two input references and no `self`, elision can't decide which one the output borrows from.

questions.question: Which lifetime elision rule applies to methods?
options: If there is `&self` or `&mut self`, its lifetime is given to all elided output lifetimes
Outputs get the shortest input lifetime
questions.answer: If there is `&self` or `&mut self`, its lifetime is given to all elided output lifetimes
questions.explanation: The rules: each elided input gets its own lifetime; a single input lifetime goes to all outputs; with `&self`, `self`'s goes to the outputs.

questions.question: What lifetime do string literals have?
questions.explanation: Literals are stored in the binary and live for the whole program: their type is `&'static str`.

questions.question: What does the bound `T: 'static` mean?
options: `T` holds no references shorter than `'static`, so owned types like `String` satisfy it
Values of `T` live until the program ends
questions.answer: `T` holds no references shorter than `'static`, so owned types like `String` satisfy it
questions.explanation: A common misconception: `T: 'static` means it *could* be kept forever. `thread::spawn` requires it for this reason.

questions.question: What does `struct Parser<'a> { input: &'a str }` guarantee?
options: A `Parser` can't outlive the string it borrows
The string lives as long as the Parser
The Parser owns a copy of the string
questions.answer: A `Parser` can't outlive the string it borrows
questions.explanation: The lifetime parameter ties the struct's validity to the borrowed data.

options: `y` has its own, unrelated lifetime, so it can't be returned as `&'a str`
Strings can't be returned by reference
questions.answer: `y` has its own, unrelated lifetime, so it can't be returned as `&'a str`
questions.explanation: The signature promises a result that lives as long as `x`; `y` might not.

questions.question: `&'a mut T` is ___ in `T`.
questions.answer: invariant
questions.explanation: If `&mut T` were covariant in `T`, you could write a shorter-lived value through it and later read it as the longer-lived type.

questions.question: What does it mean that `&'a T` is covariant in `'a`?
options: A reference with a longer lifetime can be used where a shorter one is expected
A shorter lifetime can be used where a longer one is expected
questions.answer: A reference with a longer lifetime can be used where a shorter one is expected
questions.explanation: `&'static str` can be passed where `&'a str` is expected: subtyping by lifetime.

questions.question: What syntax introduces a higher-ranked trait bound, as in `F: ___ Fn(&'a str) -> &'a str`?
questions.explanation: `for<'a>` says the bound holds for every lifetime `'a`, which closures taking references need.

questions.question: With `impl<'a> Iterator for Words<'a> { type Item = &'a str; ... }`, what do the items borrow from?
options: The original string that `Words` borrows, so items can outlive the iterator
questions.answer: The original string that `Words` borrows, so items can outlive the iterator
questions.explanation: Items tied to `'a` rather than to `&mut self` are why `collect` works. A 'lending iterator' whose items borrow the iterator needs GATs.

questions.question: What is `'_`?
options: The anonymous (elided) lifetime, as in `impl fmt::Display for Wrapper<'_>`
A lifetime that is always invalid
questions.answer: The anonymous (elided) lifetime, as in `impl fmt::Display for Wrapper<'_>`
questions.explanation: `'_` makes an elided lifetime visible, and is recommended in paths like `Formatter<'_>`.

questions.question: What does the bound `T: 'a` mean?
questions.answer: Every reference inside `T` outlives `'a`
questions.explanation: An outlives bound: `T` may be kept around for `'a` without any of its borrows expiring.

questions.question: In the 2024 edition, what does return-position `impl Trait` capture by default?
options: All in-scope generic parameters, including lifetimes
questions.answer: All in-scope generic parameters, including lifetimes
questions.explanation: Rust 2024 made RPIT capture every in-scope lifetime; `impl Trait + use<'a, T>` (precise capturing, stable since 1.82) narrows it.

tests.title: 04 · Structs, enums and pattern matching
tests.description: Data modelling with structs and enums, and matching on them.

questions.question: What happens if a `match` doesn't cover every possible value?
options: It doesn't compile: matches must be exhaustive
The unmatched values panic at run time
questions.answer: It doesn't compile: matches must be exhaustive
questions.explanation: Exhaustiveness checking is why adding an enum variant points you at every `match` that must handle it.

questions.question: In the pattern `Some(ref name)`, what does `ref` do?
options: Binds by reference instead of moving the value out
questions.answer: Binds by reference instead of moving the value out
questions.explanation: With match ergonomics it's rarely needed: matching on `&Option<String>` binds by reference automatically.

questions.question: Which symbol binds a value while also testing it against a pattern, as in `n ___ 1..=9 => ...`?
questions.explanation: `n @ 1..=9` binds `n` only if the value is in the range.

questions.question: What is `let Some(x) = opt else { return; };` called?
questions.answer: let-else
questions.explanation: Stable since Rust 1.65: bind on success, and the `else` block must diverge (return, break, continue or panic).

questions.question: When matching `&Option<String>` with the pattern `Some(s)`, what type does `s` get?
questions.answer: `&String`
questions.explanation: Match ergonomics (default binding modes): matching through a reference binds by reference.

questions.question: How large is an enum like `enum Shape { Circle { r: f64 }, Square(f64) }`?
options: Big enough for its largest variant plus a tag, unless a niche lets the tag be stored inside a field
The sum of all variants' sizes
questions.answer: Big enough for its largest variant plus a tag, unless a niche lets the tag be stored inside a field
questions.explanation: Enums are tagged unions; niche optimization can fold the tag into invalid bit patterns of a field.

questions.question: What is the status of let chains, `if let Some(x) = a && x > 0 { ... }`?
options: Stable in the 2024 edition, since Rust 1.88
questions.answer: Stable in the 2024 edition, since Rust 1.88
questions.explanation: Let chains were stabilized in Rust 1.88 for edition 2024 crates, which also changed `if let` temporary scopes.

questions.question: What does `matches!(value, Some(1..=9))` return?
questions.answer: A `bool`
questions.explanation: `matches!` is a macro that expands to a `match` returning true or false, and it supports guards.

questions.question: What does `#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]` on a struct require?
options: Every field's type implements those traits
The struct has no generic parameters
questions.answer: Every field's type implements those traits
questions.explanation: Derives generate field-by-field implementations. For generic structs they also add bounds like `T: Clone`.

questions.question: `let c = Config { verbose: true, ..base };` What happens to `base`?
options: Its remaining fields move into `c`; `base` is unusable afterwards if any moved field isn't `Copy`
questions.answer: Its remaining fields move into `c`; `base` is unusable afterwards if any moved field isn't `Copy`
questions.explanation: Struct update syntax moves or copies the other fields out of `base`.

questions.question: What is a struct with no fields, like `struct Marker;`, called?
questions.explanation: Unit structs take no space: they are zero-sized and useful as markers or trait implementors.

questions.question: How are match guards (`Some(n) if n > 5 => ...`) treated for exhaustiveness?
options: Guards are not considered, so a catch-all arm is still needed
The compiler proves the guards cover everything
questions.answer: Guards are not considered, so a catch-all arm is still needed
questions.explanation: The checker doesn't reason about guard conditions; add `_ =>` or an unguarded arm.

questions.question: What's the difference between `_` and `_name` in a pattern?
options: `_` doesn't bind, so nothing is moved; `_name` binds (and moves) but silences the unused warning
`_` moves the value and drops it at once
questions.answer: `_` doesn't bind, so nothing is moved; `_name` binds (and moves) but silences the unused warning
questions.explanation: Also, `let _ = m.lock().unwrap();` drops the new guard at once, while `let _guard = m.lock().unwrap();` keeps it until the scope ends: a classic locking bug.

questions.question: How do you match a `String` against string literal patterns?
questions.answer: Match on `s.as_str()`
questions.explanation: Literal patterns are `&str`, so match on a `&str` view of the String.

questions.question: What does `#[non_exhaustive]` on a public enum mean for other crates?
options: Their matches must include a wildcard arm, so new variants can be added without a breaking change
The enum can't be matched at all
questions.answer: Their matches must include a wildcard arm, so new variants can be added without a breaking change
questions.explanation: Within the defining crate it behaves normally. It's the tool for evolvable error enums.

options: It doesn't compile: the guard makes the match non-exhaustive
questions.answer: `"small odd"`
questions.explanation: Arms are tried top to bottom: the guard fails for 7, so the range arm matches. The `_` arm keeps the match exhaustive.

tests.title: 05 · Traits and generics
tests.description: Defining and implementing traits, generic code and its rules.

questions.question: What does the orphan rule say?
options: You can implement a trait for a type only if the trait or the type is defined in your crate
Traits can't be implemented for types in other modules
Every trait needs at least one implementation
questions.answer: You can implement a trait for a type only if the trait or the type is defined in your crate
questions.explanation: Coherence: it guarantees at most one impl per trait and type across the whole dependency graph.

questions.question: When should a trait use an associated type (`type Item;`) rather than a generic parameter?
options: When each implementing type has exactly one natural choice, like an iterator's item
When the trait has to support many types at once
Associated types are just shorter to write
questions.answer: When each implementing type has exactly one natural choice, like an iterator's item
questions.explanation: `Iterator` has one `Item` per implementor. A generic trait like `From<T>` can be implemented many times for one type.

questions.question: `impl<T: Display> ToString for T { ... }` is an example of what?
questions.answer: A blanket implementation
questions.explanation: A blanket impl covers every type meeting the bounds; that's why any `Display` type has `to_string()`.

questions.question: What is `fn show(x: impl Display)` equivalent to?
options: `fn show<T: Display>(x: T)`, except callers can't name `T` with a turbofish
A function taking any type at all
questions.answer: `fn show<T: Display>(x: T)`, except callers can't name `T` with a turbofish
questions.explanation: Argument-position `impl Trait` is an anonymous generic parameter, dispatched statically.

questions.question: What does return-position `impl Iterator<Item = u32>` promise?
options: One concrete type, which callers can't name
A different type on each call
questions.answer: One concrete type, which callers can't name
questions.explanation: All return paths must produce the same concrete type; to return different types, box them or use an enum.

questions.question: What is the compiler's process of generating a separate copy of generic code for each concrete type called?
questions.explanation: It makes generics zero-cost at run time but costs compile time and code size.

questions.question: What is a supertrait, as in `trait Loud: Display { ... }`?
options: A requirement: implementing `Loud` requires also implementing `Display`
questions.answer: A requirement: implementing `Loud` requires also implementing `Display`
questions.explanation: Supertraits are bounds on `Self`; `Loud`'s default methods may use `Display`'s methods.

questions.question: What does `T: ?Sized` mean in a bound?
options: `T` may be a dynamically sized type such as `str`, `[u8]` or `dyn Trait`
`T` can be any size up to a pointer
questions.answer: `T` may be a dynamically sized type such as `str`, `[u8]` or `dyn Trait`
questions.explanation: Generic parameters are implicitly `Sized`; `?Sized` relaxes that, so `T` can only be used behind a pointer.

questions.question: Can a trait declare associated constants, such as `const MAX: u32;`?
options: Yes, and implementors give the value
questions.answer: Yes, and implementors give the value
questions.explanation: Associated consts are resolved per type at compile time.

questions.question: When do you need the fully qualified form `<Type as Trait>::method(&x)`?
options: When several traits give the type a method with the same name, or for associated functions with no `self`
Whenever you call a trait method
questions.answer: When several traits give the type a method with the same name, or for associated functions with no `self`
questions.explanation: It removes ambiguity about which trait's method is meant.

questions.question: You want `Display` for `Vec<MyType>`. What's the idiomatic way?
options: Wrap it in a newtype, `struct MyList(Vec<MyType>);`, and implement `Display` for that
questions.answer: Wrap it in a newtype, `struct MyList(Vec<MyType>);`, and implement `Display` for that
questions.explanation: Both `Display` and `Vec` are foreign, so the orphan rule forbids the direct impl.

questions.question: You want conversions both ways between `A` and `B`. What should you implement?
options: `From<A> for B` (and `From<B> for A`); `Into` comes for free
questions.answer: `From<A> for B` (and `From<B> for A`); `Into` comes for free
questions.explanation: A blanket `impl<T, U: From<T>> Into<U> for T` exists, so implementing `From` is preferred.

questions.question: Which of these are auto traits, implemented automatically when every field implements them?
questions.answer: `Send`, `Sync` and `Unpin`
questions.explanation: Auto traits are structural: a raw-pointer field opts a type out of `Send` and `Sync`, and `PhantomPinned` out of `Unpin`.

questions.question: A trait adds a method with a default body in a new version. Is that a breaking change for implementors?
options: No: existing implementations inherit the default
Yes: every implementor must add it
Only if the method is generic
questions.answer: No: existing implementations inherit the default
questions.explanation: Semver treats it as minor (it could, rarely, cause ambiguous method names). A new method *without* a default breaks implementors.

questions.answer: `inherent`
questions.explanation: Inherent methods win over trait methods of the same name. `Greet::hi(&A)` calls the trait's.

tests.title: 06 · Trait objects and dynamic dispatch
tests.description: `dyn Trait`, vtables, dyn compatibility and when to use them.

questions.question: How big is a `&dyn Trait` on a 64-bit target?
options: 16 bytes: a data pointer and a vtable pointer
Whatever the concrete type's size is
questions.answer: 16 bytes: a data pointer and a vtable pointer
questions.explanation: Trait-object references are fat pointers; the vtable holds the method pointers, size, alignment and drop glue.

questions.question: Which method in a trait stops it being used as `dyn Trait` (unless it has `where Self: Sized`)?
questions.answer: `fn duplicate(&self) -> Self;`
questions.explanation: Returning `Self` by value needs the concrete size. Mark such methods `where Self: Sized` to keep the trait dyn compatible.

questions.question: What does a generic method, `fn visit<T>(&self, t: T)`, do to a trait's dyn compatibility?
options: Makes it not dyn compatible, unless the method has `where Self: Sized`
questions.answer: Makes it not dyn compatible, unless the method has `where Self: Sized`
questions.explanation: A vtable can't hold an entry for every possible `T`.

questions.question: What was 'dyn compatibility' called before the Rust docs renamed it?
questions.explanation: The same rules; 'dyn compatible' describes them more precisely.

questions.question: What is the trade-off of `&dyn Trait` compared with generics?
options: One compiled copy and a smaller binary, but an indirect call that usually can't be inlined
It can't be stored in collections
questions.answer: One compiled copy and a smaller binary, but an indirect call that usually can't be inlined
questions.explanation: Generics monomorphize, which is fast but bigger; `dyn` shares code at the cost of indirection.

questions.question: Why do error types in async code so often carry `+ Send + Sync`, as in `Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>`?
options: So the error can move across threads, as in tasks on a multi-threaded runtime
It makes errors cheaper to create
So the error can be printed
questions.answer: So the error can move across threads, as in tasks on a multi-threaded runtime
questions.explanation: A plain `Box<dyn Error>` isn't `Send`, which makes futures holding it `!Send`.

questions.question: Since Rust 1.86, can `&dyn Sub` be coerced to `&dyn Super` when `trait Sub: Super`?
questions.answer: Yes: trait upcasting is stable
questions.explanation: Trait upcasting coercion was stabilized in Rust 1.86, so `&dyn Sub` converts to `&dyn Super` directly.

questions.question: `Box<dyn Trait>` is shorthand for which type?
questions.answer: `Box<dyn Trait + 'static>`
questions.explanation: The default object lifetime bound for Box is `'static`, which is why boxing a borrowed value needs an explicit lifetime.

questions.question: What is needed to downcast a `&dyn Any` with `downcast_ref::<T>()`?
questions.answer: `T: 'static`
questions.explanation: `Any` depends on `TypeId`, which only exists for `'static` types.

questions.question: When is an enum usually better than trait objects?
options: When the set of variants is closed and known up front
When third parties must add new cases
Never: trait objects are always better
questions.answer: When the set of variants is closed and known up front
questions.explanation: Enums allow exhaustive matching and no allocation; trait objects suit open-ended extension.

questions.question: `fn f<T: Trait>(t: &T)`. Can you call `f(obj)` with `obj: &dyn Trait`?
options: Only if the bound is relaxed to `T: Trait + ?Sized`
questions.answer: Only if the bound is relaxed to `T: Trait + ?Sized`
questions.explanation: `dyn Trait` is unsized, so it can't satisfy the implicit `T: Sized`. `dyn Trait` itself implements `Trait` when the trait is dyn compatible.

questions.question: How is a method called on `Box<dyn Shape>` dispatched?
options: Through a function pointer in the vtable, chosen at run time
By a string lookup of the method name
By pattern matching on the type
questions.answer: Through a function pointer in the vtable, chosen at run time
questions.explanation: That's dynamic dispatch; generics give static dispatch.

tests.title: 07 · Standard library traits
tests.description: The traits every Rust type is expected to know about.

questions.question: Why doesn't `f64` implement `Eq`?
questions.answer: `NaN != NaN`, so equality isn't reflexive
